fields.meta_title: Photo Release Form Builder and Sample Wording | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a photo release form that asks about each use, takes parent signatures for minors and tells photographers whom to skip. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Photo Release Form That Records Each Person's Choices
fields.hero_description: Create a photo release form with a yes or no for every use, parent signatures for minors, and one database of answers.
fields.features_heading: The Parts of a Photo Release Worth Getting Right
fields.features_subheading: Months after the shoot, someone will ask who agreed to which use. Each part below answers that.
fields.feature_1:
A checkbox for each use

List every place a photo could run, such as the newsletter or a paid ad. People tick the uses they accept, and each tick is stored as its own field you can filter and search.
fields.feature_2:
Parent signatures for minors

Ask for the signer's date of birth first. Anyone under the age you set goes to a page their parent or guardian completes, with the child's name and the parent's relationship saved.
fields.feature_3:
A do-not-photograph list on request

Give photographers a list of everyone who declined, with a class or badge number beside each name. The list changes the moment a new release is signed or an old one is withdrawn.
fields.feature_4:
Withdrawals that reach the right person

Let anyone withdraw through a link in their copy. The record is marked withdrawn with the date, and whoever runs your website gets an email listing the photos tagged with them.
fields.feature_5:
A signed PDF in every inbox

Email each signer a PDF of the release showing their choices and signature. The same file stays in your database beside their answers for the day someone asks what they agreed to.
fields.feature_6:
Code that leaves with you

On paid plans, export the full source code of the release form to your GitHub. A developer can host it on your own servers or connect it to the registration system you run.

fields.tab_content_1:
The photographer knows which 3 students to skip

Parents sign the release at enrollment, one form per child. On picture day the photographer opens the Room 12 roster on a tablet, with 3 of its 24 students marked in red. Their parents said no. The yearbook team sees the same 3 names before any candid shot goes to print.
fields.tab_content_2:
Opt out at registration, then wear a red dot

Registration for the Harbor Ops Summit asks every attendee one question about cameras. This year 18 of 420 attendees said no. Their badges print with a red dot, and the event photographer gets their badge numbers before the doors open.
fields.tab_content_3:
Bulletin, yes. Livestream, no.

Hillcrest families answer per channel: the printed bulletin, the church website and the Sunday livestream. The Moran family allows the bulletin and declines the website and livestream. Before anything is posted, the media team searches a family name and sees each answer.
fields.tab_content_4:
When someone withdraws, their photos come off the site

A volunteer at Northwind Food Bank withdraws her release through the link in her signed copy. The communications lead gets an email listing the 6 website photos tagged with her name. Each one is marked for removal, and her volunteer record keeps the date she withdrew.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Photo Release Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan and word a photo release form, then build it with Emergent so every signed choice lands in your database.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write the release in plain words
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Decide who acts on the answers
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with who will appear in the photos. Adults sign for themselves. New York and California both require a parent or guardian to consent before a minor's picture is used in advertising. Give minors a separate path that collects the parent's details and signature.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Ask for each use on its own line, with paid advertising kept apart from the newsletter. Separate lines let a parent accept the yearbook and still turn down an ad campaign. Add one more line stating how long the permission lasts.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write the release in everyday words a parent reads in one pass. State whether anyone is paid for the photos. Explain how to withdraw and what a withdrawal changes. A dense legal paragraph tends to get signed without being read.
fields.howto_step_4_des: List the people who need the answers on the day itself: the photographer, the yearbook editor, whoever posts to social media. Each one needs the people who declined, sorted the way they work, by class or by badge number.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your release wording into the prompt, then list the uses and the age rule. Emergent builds the form and the database behind it. Name the people who get notified about withdrawals, and change any part of the form later by prompting.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Email every signer a PDF of what they signed. Send the photographer the do-not-photograph list the night before a shoot. Post a Slack message or send an email to your web editor whenever someone withdraws a release.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Fill the form as the parent of a 9-year-old and decline social media before signing. Open the PDF, then confirm the child appears on the photographer's list. Have a lawyer read the wording before the first real family signs it.

plan.angle: The top 10 is mostly static paper: Word and PDF samples from the Redwoods Group, the Federal Bar Association, the ADA and GLOBE, Adobe's explainer and template pages from AidaForm and Lightfolio. None of them deal with what happens after the signature: which uses a person agreed to, who signed for a minor, and how the photographer knows whom to leave out. This page gives sample wording and the parts every release needs, then shows the release as a working app: a choice per use, a parent's signature for minors, a do-not-photograph list for picture day and events, and each signed release kept beside the photos it covers.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Photo Release Form That Records Each Person's Choices', title 'Photo Release Form Builder and Sample Wording | Emergent' and hero 'Create a photo release form with a yes or no for every use, parent signatures for minors, and one database of answers.' cover the whole job; hero under 130 chars; how-to description is one sentence.

intent.evidence: Builder-fit SERP served: sample wording (FAQ 5), what a release must include (FAQ 4), why it is needed with NY and CA law (FAQ 3), a seven-step how-to and the builder; the title's 'Sample Wording' promise is delivered in FAQ 5.

specificity.evidence: Buyer detail: 'Room 12 roster ... 3 of its 24 students marked in red', '18 of 420 attendees said no', 'printed bulletin, the church website and the Sunday livestream', '6 website photos tagged with her name'.

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: 'Parents sign the release at enrollment...', 'Registration for the Harbor Ops Summit asks...', 'List every place a photo could run...'.

craft.evidence: Short declaratives, one idea each; QC Q5 clean. Repeated ideas logged as notes.

voice.evidence: Reads like an operator wrote it: 'Months after the shoot, someone will ask who agreed to which use.'

truth.evidence: Two fields stretch the code-export claim into exporting signed records: feature_6 'On paid plans, export the release form and every signed record to your GitHub.' and FAQ 7 'Emergent's code export on paid plans lets you hold those records in your own GitHub repository.' Legal facts (NY Civil Rights Law 50, CA Civil Code 3344 and its news exemption) match domain_sources.

distinct.evidence: Sibling primaries (liability waiver form, consent form) appear only as FAQ links; model release form is not targeted; tabs are distinct segments (school, conference, church, nonprofit).

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions, answered first; no brand or format in a question; hub link in item 2; two sibling links; moat lines in items 7 and 9 (item 7 carries the truth defect above).

images.evidence: Contact sheet matches copy: '3 of 24 students' and 'Yearbook sees the same 3' (tab 1), '18 of 420' and 'Red dot on the badge' (tab 2), 'Bulletin, yes. Website and livestream, no.' (tab 3), '6 website photos' and 'Emailed to the communications lead' (tab 4).

findings.quote: On paid plans, export the release form and every signed record to your GitHub.
findings.issue: The ledger claim 'code-export' is full code export to GitHub; it does not say signed records (database rows, personal data) go to the repository. This states a capability beyond rules/capabilities.json (CONTENT_DEFECTS #14).
findings.fix: Export only the code: 'On paid plans, export the full source of the release form to your GitHub.' Keep records in the database you own.

findings.quote: Emergent's code export on paid plans lets you hold those records in your own GitHub repository.
findings.issue: Same class in FAQ item 7: code export is presented as a way to keep the signed release records, which the code-export claim does not cover.
findings.fix: Use an approved moat that fits record keeping, e.g. 'An Emergent form keeps every signed release in a database you own.'
